subject: math
objective: Explain why equivalent ratios describe the same mix (both quantities are multiplied or divided by the same number, while adding the same amount to both changes the ratio); find missing values in ratio and rate problems using a ratio table, a double number line, a scale factor, or a unit rate; compare rates by finding unit rates; distinguish part-to-part ratios from part-to-whole fractions; and decide whether a relationship is proportional from a table (constant y ÷ x) or a graph (a straight line through the origin), giving the constant of proportionality k in y = kx.
prerequisites: Multiplying and dividing whole numbers and decimals
Simple fractions and fraction of a quantity
Reading a table and plotting points on a coordinate grid
standardsNote: TBD. Ratios, rates, and proportional relationships are common grade 6 and grade 7 topics, but no Oklahoma Academic Standards code has been checked. Verify against https://oklahoma.gov/education/services/standards-learning/oklahoma-academic-standards.html with the teacher before attaching codes.
sources: OpenStax, Prealgebra 2e, Section 5.6: Ratios and Rate (definitions of ratio, rate, unit rate, and unit price) (https://openstax.org/books/prealgebra-2e/pages/5-6-ratios-and-rate)

OpenStax, Prealgebra 2e, Section 6.5: Solve Proportions and their Applications (definition of a proportion and solving with equal cross products) (https://openstax.org/books/prealgebra-2e/pages/6-5-solve-proportions-and-their-applications)

Illustrative Mathematics, IM 6–8 Math, Grade 7 Unit 2: Introducing Proportional Relationships, unit teacher guide (definitions of proportional relationship and constant of proportionality; CC BY-NC 4.0) (https://illustrativemathematics.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/Grade7-2-Unit-teacher-guide.pdf)
misconceptions: Additive reasoning: adding the same amount to both parts keeps a ratio the same (2 : 3 and 4 : 5)
Taking the same amount away from both parts simplifies a ratio (6 : 4 to 4 : 2)
Order in a ratio doesn't matter (2 : 5 is the same as 5 : 2)
A part-to-part ratio is the fraction of the whole (in 2 : 3, blue is 2/3 of the paint)
The mix with more of something has a bigger share of it (5 : 8 is bluer than 3 : 4 because 5 > 3)
Whoever goes farther is faster, regardless of time; the bigger package or the lower total price is the better buy
A unit rate can be divided either way without changing its meaning (miles per gallon vs gallons per mile)
Any relationship where both quantities increase, or any straight-line graph, is proportional (taxi fare with a starting fee)
Any graph through the origin is proportional (area of a square)
The constant of proportionality is x ÷ y, or the jump between two table columns
modelLimitations: The paint colors come from one number only, the share of blue in the bucket, interpolated along a hand-picked blue-to-yellow gradient. Real paints mix by more complicated rules; the model is a simplification chosen so that same ratio means same color.
The paint mixer allows 0 to 15 cans of each color; missions use small whole numbers.
Ratio tables offer ×2, ×3, ×10, ÷2, and 'Make it 1'; non-terminating decimals are shown as mixed numbers such as 2 2/3.
The double number lines put both lines on one scale so equivalent pairs line up; overlapping labels are hidden, and the selected and answered rows are always labeled.
Runners in the race move at constant speed, which real runners don't; speeds are whole meters per second from 3 to 8.
Unit prices in the better-buy comparison are whole cents per ounce, and ounces per dollar are rounded to two decimal places.
Typed answers may be whole numbers, decimals, fractions, mixed numbers, or dollar amounts; a decimal within 0.006 of a non-terminating exact answer is accepted.
Practice draws 6 of 8 problem templates with random numbers. Proportions are solved with scale factors, unit rates, and groups; cross-multiplication is not taught as a procedure.
Percent, scale drawings with area, and inversely proportional relationships are not included.
